title: Attention launch jitter autopsy
content:
Purpose:
Quick investigative notebook to capture experiments, observations, and hypotheses around sporadic latency spikes (micro-jitter) observed when running fused attention kernels (FlashAttention variants + small fused ops chain) under realistic traffic patterns. This is a working doc — lots of raw traces, blind alleys, and TODOs.

Background / symptom summary:
- Production SLO: p99 end-to-end token latency <= 120ms for small-batch chat requests (batch size 1–4).
- After deploying fused ops landing (PR linked above) we started seeing intermittent 2–6x p99 regressions on certain node types (A100-80GB, driver 535.xx). Average latency unchanged.
- Correlated with: bursty concurrent arrival patterns (small-batch tails), mixed seq-lengths in same queue, and when KV-cache hits are lower (cold conversations).
- Not a full CPU throttle or GPU OOM; GPU utilization looks normal but kernel launch latency and small-kernel throughput vary.

Hypothesis space (ranked):
1) Kernel launch jitter due to driver PCIe/IPC contention when many small kernels scheduled rapidly (small sequence lens + fused ops create many microkernels).
2) NUMA/pci bus placement causing occasional device-host DMA slowdown (pinned vs pageable memory).
3) Prefetch + fused-op scheduling race: the runtime prefetches KV blocks into scratchpads; sometimes those prefetchs are serialized and block microkernels, causing tail spikes.
4) CUDA runtime CUDAGraph replay misalignment with variable seq lengths leading to kernel rebind overheads.
5) CPU-side thread contention in the scheduler when coalescing batches leads to variable submit spacing.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Workloads: synthetic microbench harness (replayer) that creates arrival patterns: poisson (lambda 2-8 rps), burst (10 concurrent then idle), constant stream. Sequence length sets: uniform [16,64], long tail (16 most, 512 occasional). Batch size settings: 1,2,4.
- Kernels: plain attention (baseline), FlashAttention-optimized (FA-v2), fused-attn+proj chain (FA+fused) — each with/without kernel fusion flag.
- Memory modes: pageable (default), pinned host buffers, cudaHostRegister on-the-fly.
- NUMA placements: processes pinned to local NUMA vs cross-NUMA (taskset + numactl).
- Traces: combined nvprof-like kernel timestamps, lightweight eBPF skb tracing for submit times, CPU thread sampling, and perf counters: SM occupancy, L2 utilization, dram_read_bytes.

Key observations (raw):
- Kernel launch latency distribution (measured host enqueue -> kernel start): baseline plain-attn: median 120us, p99 350us. FA+fused median 150us, p99 2.8ms (spiky).
- Spikes align with bursts of small kernels: when more than ~40 microkernels are enqueued within 20ms window, p99 explodes.
- Using pinned host buffers reduces p99 by ~30% for FA+fused in burst workload (2.8ms -> ~1.9ms), suggesting pageable->pinned DMA cost matters.
- NUMA cross-placement increases spike frequency (p99 jumps ~20–40%) on dual-socket instances.
- CUDAGraph replay reduces average enqueue overhead but does not eliminate jitter when seq-lengths vary heavily (graphs need different shapes, causing fallback to immediate launch).
- When enabling a lightweight coalescing delay of 0.8ms in scheduler (intentionally group more arrivals), spikes reduce but average latency increases for non-bursty traffic.

Interpretation / tentative root causes:
- Primary: microkernel burstiness overwhelms host-GPU DMA and driver scheduling path. Flash/fused ops increase the number of distinct kernels per token (more launches) and the small-size DMA pattern amplifies PCIe latency jitter.
- Secondary: cross-NUMA host memory placement and use of pageable memory exacerbate the DMA tail.
- Tertiary: scheduler submit spacing and lack of adaptive coalescing leads to pathological submit patterns (many tiny enqueues).

Short experiments that ruled things out quickly:
- GPU power-capping: no strong correlation (spikes still present).
- Single-process vs multi-process: same binary under different numbers of processes shows spike frequency shifting but not eliminated => not purely per-process bug.

Relevant measurements (snippet):
- Example run: burst workload, FA+fused, pageable:
  - median enqueue->start: 153us
  - p95: 410us
  - p99: 2.8ms
  - sm_occupancy avg: 38%
  - dram_read_bytes spike concurrent with p99 events: +2.6x
- Same with pinned host buffers:
  - median: 140us, p99: 1.9ms (drop ~32%)

Actionable mitigations (short-term & long-term):
Short-term (ships quickly):
- Force pinned host buffers for small-batch, small-seq requests (config flag in runtime). Targets 20–40% p99 reduction in bursts. Risks: increased host memory usage and jitter in other scenarios.
- Adaptive coalescing policy: add a small randomized micro-batching delay (0.5–1.0ms) for ephemeral bursts, ramped down with concurrency. Pro: reduces microkernel bursts. Con: increases median latency slightly and requires tuning.
- NUMA-aware placement: ensure host pinned pages are local to GPU's CPU socket (numactl or explicit allocator). Low risk, clear win on dual-socket nodes.

Long-term (engineering work):
- Kernel fusion: reduce number of microkernel launches by fusing adjacent ops further upstream (but maintain numerical parity). This is roadmap-level work and interacts with quantization/fast-paths.
- DMA batching: implement batch submission of small host->device DMAs where possible (coalesce memcpy ops) at runtime allocator layer.
- Improved CUDAGraph strategy: maintain a small set of common graph shapes and fast fallback patching to avoid immediate-launch fallback cost.
- Scheduler rewrite: move to a lock-free submission queue per-GPU streamer thread to smooth host enqueue bursts.

Open questions / experiments to run next:
- Measure effect of kernel compilation / JIT cache warmness on launch spikes (are we seeing on-demand PTX->SASS fallback?). Add instrumentation for kernel binary cache hits.
- Can we reproduce on AWS p4d instances (different PCIe topology) to isolate vendor-specific driver behavior?
- Quantify memory pin overhead at cluster scale: will forcing pinned buffers push other workloads to swap or increase host memory pressure?
- Explore interleaving large-kernel requests with burst microkernels to see if scheduling fairness contributes.

Commands / quick repro notes (how to reproduce locally):
- Replayer harness (repo): tools/attn_replayer --pattern burst --arrival 50ms --batch-cap 4 --seq-dist "mixture:90@16,10@512" --kernel fa-fused --mem-mode pageable --numa cross
- Trace collection:
  - nvtx markers around enqueue/submit.
  - nsys record -t CUDA,OSRuntime --trace-fork true --output nvtrace.nsys <binary>
  - custom host-side timestamps: CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW before enqueue, after submit, kernel-start via CUPTI callback.

Notes to self / future doc hygiene:
- Create a canonical microkernel-burst benchmark in benchmarks/ that can be run on CI to prevent regressions. Include pinned vs pageable matrix.
- Pair with SRE to roll out pinned-buffer toggle behind feature flag + canary to 5% traffic. Monitor host memory footprint and p99 latency.
- Cross-link to PR that added fused ops (see linked PR) and mention this doc in the PR description to avoid regressions in future changes.

Unresolved bits and hypotheses I don’t fully trust yet:
- Some p99 spikes appear when L2 util is high—could be contention inside GPU L2 banking causing kernel start jitter (need microbench to isolate).
- Interaction with multi-stream concurrency: are we seeing stream contention (streams per request) causing sequentialization? Need to instrument stream-level queueing.

Appendix: quick timeline of experiments performed (short):
- 2024-11-16: initial reproduction and nvprof traces collected.
- 2024-11-18: pinned-memory experiment (reduced p99).
- 2024-11-21: NUMA placement tests (cross-NUMA worsens).
- 2024-11-25: CUDAGraph variation + coalescing delay tests.
- 2024-11-29: scheduler random-delay experiment (reduced spikes at cost of median).

If you are picking this up: check the benchmarks/attn-burst folder, start by reproducing pinned vs pageable runs on an A100 node. I left raw nsys traces in /mnt/prof/traces/attn-jitter-20241116 (ask SRE for access).

End of notebook (for now).
